items.title: Dolly Parton’s Sister Stella Calls Out ‘Fake AI Garbage’ & ‘Snarky Tweets’ About Singer’s Death
items.summary:
Stella Parton has asked the public to ease up on the commentary surrounding her sister's death, posting a two-slide letter to Instagram on Friday, Sept. 4, ten days after Dolly Parton died at 80. In it, she described the strain of grieving in view of strangers. "We will be okay in time but each of us will grieve in our own personal way," she wrote. "Sadly, because of the way our lives have been in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."

Much of Stella's frustration, as Billboard reported, is aimed at what has filled the vacuum online since the singer's death. "There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it's been challenging to absorb and or ignore," she wrote, before turning to the question of why her sister had spent decades declining to weigh in publicly on politics, religion or other public figures.

Stella framed that reticence as a deliberate choice rather than evasiveness. Dolly, she wrote, "loved her fans and the public in general," and understood "what a negative vortex that could turn into which is nothing but a huge waste of positive energy." She asked readers to "show more compassion and wisdom" and to "use my sister's life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others."

She closed the letter with a direct challenge to the incentives of posting. "It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she wrote. "At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself? It's not about what other individuals you will never meet think of you!"

Dolly Parton died Aug. 25 after a brief cancer battle, a diagnosis that only became public after her death. She was the fourth-oldest of 12 siblings; Stella is the sixth. Their brother Coy died earlier this year.

This is Stella's second public statement in as many weeks. Two days after her sister's death, she wrote that Dolly had been willing to let doctors try "experimental drugs" on her in the hope the research might eventually help others, adding, "My sister was one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people I've ever known. What the world saw is exactly who she was."

items.title: Lainey Wilson Set to Host 2026 CMA Awards
items.summary:
Lainey Wilson will host the 60th annual CMA Awards, making her the first woman to solo-host the show twice. The Country Music Association announced her return on Saturday, Sept. 5, during ESPN's College GameDay, timing the reveal to the program's 500th road broadcast, which came from Louisiana State University in Wilson's home state.

Wilson solo-hosted last year's ceremony after sharing 2024 duties with Luke Bryan and Peyton Manning. Dolly Parton became the first woman to solo-host in 1988, followed by Reba McEntire in 1991. Vince Gill leads all hosts with 10 solo turns, ahead of Johnny Cash with four and Tennessee Ernie Ford and Kenny Rogers with three each.

"I couldn't be more excited to be hosting the CMA Awards again this year, especially with it being the 60th anniversary," Wilson said in a statement. "I've had so much fun hosting the last two years, and this one's going to be extra special. Can't wait to see y'all in November!"

The ceremony airs live from Nashville's Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 8 p.m. ET/7 p.m. CT on ABC and Disney+, with next-day availability on Hulu. Billboard reported that nominees will be announced Thursday, Sept. 10, first on ABC's Good Morning America and then via livestream on the CMA's YouTube channel. Tickets go on sale Friday, Sept. 18 at CMAworld.com.

Wilson, 34, has won 12 CMA Awards in three years, putting her second among female artists behind Miranda Lambert's 14. The Country Music Association produces the broadcast, with Robert Deaton as executive producer, Alan Carter directing and Jon Macks as head writer. More than 7,000 professional CMA voting members determine the nominees and winners.

Bridgestone Arena has hosted the milestone shows before, including the 40th in 2006, when it was known as the Gaylord Entertainment Center and Brooks & Dunn hosted, and the 50th in 2015 with Brad Paisley and Carrie Underwood.

items.title: Robert Pattinson on Chris Hansen’s Objections to ‘Primetime’: “I Hope He Likes the Movie”
items.summary:
Robert Pattinson addressed Chris Hansen's objections to Primetime at the film's Venice Film Festival press conference this weekend, where the To Catch a Predator host loomed over the proceedings despite not attending. Hansen had raised early complaints about Lance Oppenheim's A24 film and bought pre-show advertising for his own streaming platform. "Obviously, I hope he likes the movie," Pattinson said.

Pattinson, who plays Hansen and came aboard early as a producer, said the subject wasn't the draw. "I never really set out to make a movie about Chris Hansen," he said. "I never really thought about it, and then I saw [Ajon Singh's] script, and there's something electrifying about it." He suggested the years of work the film has drawn out of its collaborators should register as a compliment of sorts.

Oppenheim told the room he came to the show sideways, through parodies on programs like South Park. "Chris Hansen was this like mythological being who had these one-liners that reminded me of Tony Montana," he said. "His version of say hello to my little friend was have a seat right there." He described being confused as a child about whether he was watching a prank show, a news show or a circus.

Singh, a first-time screenwriter, loosely adapted the script from a Luke Dittrich article in Esquire, building the film around the darkest year of Hansen's run on the series. Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers — in her first feature role — and Bokeem Woodbine costar, and all joined the panel.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, the conversation turned to memes after a journalist noted Pattinson's performance had already gone viral ahead of release. Pattinson said he welcomed it, recalling classmates who quoted Jim Carrey films and Austin Powers. "I used to know [all the lines] from The Mask by heart," he said. Oppenheim framed Hansen as "a person who became a persona, a person who embraced the meme of himself."

Pattinson is currently shooting the Batman sequel, part of a run that also includes The Drama, The Odyssey, Primetime and Dune: Part Three. He moved from Primetime to Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey within hours, and said the seam shows: "I definitely can hear a little Chris Hansen in The Odyssey when I watch it." A24 opens Primetime in U.S. theaters Sept. 25; Venice closes with its awards ceremony Sept. 12.

items.title: Yeat Appears to Diss Travis Scott on New Track “On Nothing”
items.summary:
Yeat has released a track called "On Nothing" that appears to aim at Travis Scott, arriving days after Yeat's verse quietly disappeared from Slime Language 3, the third compilation in Young Thug's YSL series. The rapper had been featured on the song "Eaters" alongside Scott, Future and Tezzus. Fans noticed the removal on Monday, Aug. 31.

In the days after, speculation held that another artist on the record had pushed Young Thug to choose between Yeat's verse and their own. Pitchfork reported that the new song, which arrived with a music video, reads as Yeat identifying who that was.

The track repeatedly targets a "Flame," a likely reference to Scott's La Flame nickname. The chorus runs "I'ma put out that flame, it's fuckin' lame," and a later verse continues the image: "I don't fuck with Flame, not a lot to say, if I saw a candle, I'd shush it / What more could I say?"

Neither Scott nor Young Thug has publicly addressed the removal or the song. Yeat's verse remains absent from "Eaters" on Slime Language 3.

items.title: Gallagher Brothers Skip Venice Press Conference for Concert Doc
items.summary:
Noel and Liam Gallagher skipped the Venice Film Festival press conference for Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger, the documentary chronicling their reunion tour. The brothers turned up for a photo call and then left, handing the podium to Steven Knight, who created the documentary, and directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace.

The film follows Oasis across 12 concerts on three continents during the Live 25 tour, the band's first shows since their split in 2009. The run took in more than $400 million at the box office. Alongside the performances, the documentary includes previously unseen backstage and rehearsal footage and the first joint interviews the brothers have given in over 20 years.

Knight, best known for creating Peaky Blinders, had never made a documentary before. He said a conversation with Noel about the scale of ticket demand set the project's central question. Fans who had loved the band the first time were joined by a generation that came to the music later, and Knight wanted to understand why.

The Hollywood Reporter reported that the directors described capturing the brothers' relationship rebuilding itself in real time. Knight recounted the first rehearsal after 15 years of silence: "Liam walks in [and says] Okay, should we start? Should we go? And they go, 1234, bang." He said the Gallaghers have watched the finished film and were "beyond satisfied," though not inclined to discuss it further.

Southern and Lovelace, who previously made the LCD Soundsystem film Shut Up and Play the Hits and the Blur documentary No Distance Left to Run, also tracked several devoted fans around the world. Lovelace pointed to audiences in South Korea, where young people born long after the songs were written have formed a deep attachment to them.

Asked whether the reconciliation might not hold, Lovelace said, "Is it going to happen again? It doesn't appear to be. You know, they seem to get on pretty well." Disney opens the film in select Imax and U.S. theaters on Sept. 11, with streaming to follow later this year on Hulu in the U.S. and on Disney+ internationally.
